assessment.nobel_worthiness: A km3-scale detector instrumenting Antarctic ice opened neutrino astronomy as a real observational window. The 2013 discovery of a diffuse astrophysical flux, then the TXS 0506+056 association, NGC 1068 and the Galactic-plane neutrinos, show a clear, original and lasting result built on decades of detector development.
assessment.attribution: Halzen drove the concept and the collaboration, Spiering was a pioneer of the neutrino-telescope programme (Baikal, AMANDA, IceCube) and Karle was central to detector construction and the ice work. A fair one-to-three prize is possible, but the leadership of a huge collaboration and the AMANDA/Baikal precursors make the allocation debatable.
assessment.maturity: Independently supported by several analyses and multi-messenger associations, with the diffuse flux confirmed across channels. The sources are only partly identified, but the discovery of the flux itself is mature and timely.
uncertainties: Source identification is still incomplete, so the astrophysical interpretation is evolving.
Credit among IceCube leaders, AMANDA and Baikal pioneers and others is not cleanly separable.
My recollection of individual roles is from general knowledge and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson by ATLAS and CMS completed the Standard Model's particle content and is a monumental detector and analysis achievement. Its worth is beyond question, though the 2013 prize already recognised the theory.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over two experiments and thousands of people. Founding leaders (Jenni, Della Negra) and the spokesperson at discovery (Gianotti) can represent ATLAS and CMS, but Virdee is an equally defensible choice and the committee must justify excluding him. Any choice is a compromise with the Nobel rules.
assessment.maturity: Observed independently by two experiments and confirmed through properties measured in Run 2. Recognition is well within timing norms, with no maturity concerns.
uncertainties: Individual attribution within very large collaborations is inherently contentious.
The 2013 prize partly absorbed the recognition, which could lower the appetite for a second Higgs prize.
Choosing three of four credited names leaves one leading figure out.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and are redefining time and enabling tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. A decisive precision instrument with broad influence.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated it, while Ye pushed the performance to the current frontier. The two-person credit is clean, though others (such as ion-clock and optical-frequency-comb pioneers) were already honoured in 2005.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have reproduced the performance and comparisons across clocks are routine. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so the field is mature but evolving.
uncertainties: AMO precision measurement is outside my core expertise and I would rely on colleagues.
Overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the ion-clock community could complicate credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Neutron-star mergers as sites of r-process nucleosynthesis, shown by the kilonova after GW170817 and earlier GRB afterglow candidates, link gravitational waves, nuclear physics and astronomy. A strong multi-messenger result with clear scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Metzger's early kilonova theory and Kasen's opacity and radiative-transfer models underpin the interpretation, while Berger led key observational detections. Other contributors (e.g. Piran, Tanvir, Li and Paczynski) also had decisive roles, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: GW170817 gave a single well-observed event with strong support, but the r-process yield and the fraction of heavy elements from mergers are not yet settled. Recognition is reasonably timely but the evidence base is thin.
uncertainties: Only one gravitational-wave-confirmed kilonova exists.
Credit between theory, modelling and observation is unresolved and the GW detector builders were already honoured in 2017.
Fraction of r-process material from mergers versus other sites remains uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration correction in electron microscopy delivered sub-angstrom resolution and atomic-scale imaging of materials, a transformative instrument that overcame a decades-old theoretical limit. It is a fine example of an enabling technique.
assessment.attribution: Rose supplied the theory of the correctors, Haider led the corrector implementation and Urban demonstrated the aberration-corrected TEM and later applications. The trio is well supported by prior prizes (Kavli, Wolf), giving a clean allocation.
assessment.maturity: Widely adopted and mature; the impact on materials science has been demonstrated for about two decades. If anything, the recognition is overdue.
uncertainties: A microscopy invention may be judged to fall more naturally under chemistry, with an eligibility question for physics.
Contributions of other groups (e.g. Krivanek, Dahmen) complicate a three-person split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP's all-sky microwave maps pinned down the cosmological parameters to percent level, establishing the standard LCDM model with a flat universe, and an age of 13.8 billion years. It made cosmology a precision science and is instrument-driven science at its best.
assessment.attribution: Bennett led the mission as principal investigator, Page led key instrument design and Spergel the analysis of the cosmological parameters. This is a defensible and reasonably clean allocation, though Planck and COBE heritage and previous prizes (2006, 2019) crowd the field.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by Planck and other experiments. Recognition is somewhat late and the topic partly covered by earlier cosmology prizes.
uncertainties: Earlier prizes for CMB anisotropy and cosmology reduce the room for another.
Credit within a large mission team (e.g. Wilkinson, Hinshaw, Komatsu) is not clearly separable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are a technical triumph of VLBI at 1.3 mm and a direct test of strong-field gravity. Vivid for the public and scientifically important.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow and Doeleman led the VLBI array development and the collaboration. Narayan's theoretical modelling is also important, so the three-name option exists, but a two-person pairing is most coherent.
assessment.maturity: The images are reproduced across epochs and for two sources but the interpretation of spin and jet physics is still under analysis. Recognition is timely, if slightly early.
uncertainties: Credit within a 200-person collaboration is hard to apportion.
Image reconstruction choices and interpretation of black-hole spin remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays opens an entirely new gravitational-wave band and is a long-baseline precision timing achievement.
assessment.attribution: Credit is shared among several PTA collaborations (EPTA, NANOGrav, PPTA, CPTA, IPTA). Kramer, McLaughlin and Siemens are plausible leaders but the allocation among collaborations is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 evidence is at roughly 3-4 sigma, with the Hellings-Downs correlation not firmly established and the source (supermassive black-hole binaries versus new physics) unresolved. Likely premature for 2026.
uncertainties: Detection significance is below the discovery standard of five sigma.
Allocation across competing collaborations is unresolved.
Interpretation of the signal source is open.
